source.title: FixNorm: Dissecting Weight Decay for Training Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Yu-Cong Zhou; Yunxiao Sun; Zhaobai Zhong

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure values are described in text; no missing or cut-off sections affect the extracted results.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how removing weight decay and controlling weight norms affects held-out classification performance, including ImageNet, Cityscapes, and MS COCO. These experiments concern regularization and generalization but do not test the specific behaviors or measures in the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out performance for weight-decay and FixNorm training and measures mean cross-boundary risk (MCBR). It does not test random-label memorization, width past interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected networks, adaptive optimizers, batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. No claim version directly matches its experiments; relevant results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study tests weight decay and FixNorm, which do not match any listed version. It does not vary dropout, optimizer family, batch size, or width past interpolation, compare convolutional with fully connected networks, or measure random-label fitting, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Its citations to related original sources do not constitute tests.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute weight decay's effects to effective learning rate in normalized layers and cross-boundary risk in the final classifier. They propose FixNorm to control both and report matching or improved held-out performance, together with an efficient hyperparameter-tuning procedure.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes FixNorm, which removes weight decay from selected layers and controls convolutional weight norms and the final classifier's scale; it uses NAG, ImageNet classification, and additional Cityscapes and MS COCO experiments. It does not reproduce any listed claim version's intervention or measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that optimal learning rate and α differ among models and settings; cosine learning rate changes the reported Cityscapes and MS COCO results. It also reports different FixNorm outcomes for the unconstrained WN-FC and constrained FixNorm-FC variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixing the convolutional weight norm while retaining final-FC weight decay matches weight-decay training at 77.8% ImageNet accuracy after learning-rate searches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Global convolutional norm fixing can replace convolutional weight decay in this batch-normalized ResNet50 setup.

fits_no_version.finding: An unconstrained weight-normalized classifier reaches 76.5% accuracy versus 77.8% with final-FC weight decay; constraining its scale restores 77.8% and maintains lower MCBR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Controlling final-classifier scale can improve boundary proximity and held-out accuracy in the tested ResNet50 setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Tuned FixNorm exceeds the stated reference metrics across the reported classification, segmentation, and detection setups, and exceeds BO+WD on two ImageNet models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tuned FixNorm can improve held-out performance over the tested reference training recipes.

record.problems: The reported comparisons use held-out validation metrics, but do not report training error, so a training-test gap cannot be assessed. The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for these results. Some comparisons in Figures 1 and 2 are described in text rather than supported by numerical tables.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. The paper mentions related work and supplementary analyses, but cited results from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including tuning, decoupled decay, and optimizer switching.
Large versus small batches under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout interventions, small-data and excessive-dropout regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All rows fall outside V1–V8; their cannot_determine states indicate lack of a matching claim measure, not unreadable results. These findings can remain under fits_no_version but should not serve as claim-verdict rows. The paper inconsistently references algorithm numbers; identify methods by their operations.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; no random-label experiment.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers compared with SGD or momentum SGD.
Batch-size comparisons and large-batch generalization gap.
Dropout interventions and their effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Weight decay on convolution and final fully connected layers compared with fixing the convolution weight norm while retaining final-layer weight decay.

conditions.value: 0.4 for WD training; grid-searched for both methods

rows.value: 77.8% for Algo 1 (fixed convolution norm; final FC weight decay retained)
rows.note: The paper says the two methods achieve the same top-1 accuracy.
rows.check: The equal 77.8% accuracies concern replacement of convolutional weight decay with norm fixing while retaining final-layer weight decay. They establish no listed effect; absent is inappropriate. This is a method comparison outside the claim versions.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained on ImageNet; epoch count not stated for this comparison
rows.operation_detail: Fixed convolution and combined convolution-plus-FC norms with either an unconstrained Weight Normalization FC layer or a FixNorm-FC layer.
rows.note: Comparison is against Algo 1, which retains final-FC weight decay; the paper attributes the gap to an additional effect of weight decay, but this is not a claim-version measure.
rows.check: The 76.5% versus 77.8% comparison concerns final-classifier scale control, outside all versions. Figure 2 shows 100 training epochs. The modified method fixes the combined convolution-plus-FC norm, rather than separately fixing both norms.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained on ImageNet; epoch count not stated for this comparison
rows.operation_detail: Fixed convolution and combined convolution-plus-FC norms with a FixNorm-FC layer and no final-FC weight decay.
rows.note: The authors say FixNorm-FC fully closes the accuracy gap to Algo 1.
rows.check: Restoring accuracy to 77.8% concerns FixNorm-FC, not a listed effect; observed is inappropriate. Figure 2 shows 100 epochs. The modified method fixes the combined convolution-plus-FC norm.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained on ImageNet; epoch count not stated for this comparison
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean cross-boundary risk (MCBR) while comparing Algo 1 with Algo 1@WN-FC.
rows.value: Without constraint, g continuously grows and leads to higher MCBR.
rows.note: The paper defines MCBR as a measure of boundary proximity and says higher values indicate greater likelihood of crossing class boundaries during testing; it does not report a training-test gap correlation for the claim's V7 measure.
rows.check: MCBR measures feature proximity to class boundaries, not magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps. It cannot test V7. Figure 2 shows 100 epochs.
